title_vi: Tấn công mạng theo bảy tầng OSI: tầng nào chịu đòn gì?

related.reason_vi: Tường lửa là một lớp đỡ ở mạng và giao vận.
Phiên đăng nhập và mã phiên, nền của đòn cố định phiên.

claims.evidence: Source read. Independent sources read from files fetched with raw.githubusercontent.com at pinned commits: OWASP CheatSheetSeries 1c3144a8 (Denial of Service, Session Management, Transport Layer Security), OWASP www-community ce281465 (format string, man-in-the-middle, session fixation, brute force), mdn/content a1aa79c0 (MITM, phishing, session hijacking, TCP handshake, Denial of Service; sparse clone) and torvalds/linux 32c52ec8 (Documentation/networking/ip-sysctl.rst). Three local experiments run with Python 3.13.16 on 127.0.0.1 or in memory (idle sockets against a one-worker server, an in-memory half-open queue model, a toy session store); IP spoofing and ARP spoofing were not run. RFCs, the CERT-EU white paper and Wikipedia were not reachable; OSI versus TCP/IP, how SYN cookies work and that an IP source address is set by the sender are general knowledge. No independent source was read for route table manipulation, VLAN hopping, MAC spoofing, physical tampering or electromagnetic interference.

claims.claim_vi: The source lists attacks per OSI layer: application (Pushing, malware injection, DDoS attacks), presentation (encoding/decoding vulnerabilities, format string attacks, malicious code injection), session (session hijacking, session fixation attacks, brute force attacks), transport (man-in-the-middle attacks, SYN/ACK flood), network (IP spoofing, route table manipulation, DDoS attacks), data link (MAC address spoofing, ARP spoofing, VLAN hopping), physical (wiretapping, physical tampering, electromagnetic interference). It names no defences.
claims.verified_by: Source body read; its SHA-256 (3e669b60...) and size (1098 bytes) match the values given by the lead.

claims.claim_vi: OWASP's Denial of Service cheat sheet uses the CERT-EU DDoS classification, which relies on the seven OSI layers but focuses on three attack surfaces: application, session (or protocol) and network (or volumetric); layers 1 and 2 are not in that classification and are discussed separately.
claims.verified_by: Read in full from a file fetched with raw.githubusercontent.com at the pinned commit. The CERT-EU white paper it cites was not reachable and was not read.

claims.claim_vi: Slow HTTP attacks deliver requests very slowly and fragmented so the server keeps resources waiting until the maximum concurrent connection pool is reached. OWASP's defences: a minimum ingress data rate with request-read timeouts (set too high it rejects legitimate slow clients, too low it weakens protection) and an absolute connection timeout.
claims.verified_by: Read in full from a file fetched with raw.githubusercontent.com at the pinned commit.

claims.claim_vi: OWASP names MAC flooding and ARP poisoning as data-link-layer DoS scenarios. In ARP poisoning an attacker's MAC address becomes linked to a legitimate device's IP address, so the attacker can intercept, modify or stop data meant for that IP address. Defences it names: packet filtering that inspects and blocks offending ARP packets, or static ARP tables (hard to maintain).
claims.section: Overview of potential DoS weaknesses (data layer)
claims.verified_by: Read in full from a file fetched with raw.githubusercontent.com at the pinned commit.

claims.claim_vi: OWASP describes physical-layer DoS scenarios as destruction, obstruction and malfunction of networking hardware (its example is a cut underground cable), and lists preventing single points of failure, with redundant systems, among its design concepts.
claims.verified_by: Read in full from a file fetched with raw.githubusercontent.com at the pinned commit.

claims.claim_vi: OWASP's ISP-level remediation is to filter invalid sender addresses using edge routers, to filter out IP-spoofing attacks done to bypass block lists.
claims.verified_by: Read in full from a file fetched with raw.githubusercontent.com at the pinned commit.

claims.claim_vi: That the source address field of an IP packet is filled in by the sender, and so can be filled in wrongly, is general knowledge.
claims.verified_by: Author's general knowledge; not checked against an RFC (IETF sites were not reachable). IP and ARP spoofing were not run.

claims.claim_vi: OWASP describes a format string attack as input being evaluated as a format string by a C format function such as printf; parameters like %x, %s and %n read or write process memory; the vulnerable call passes user input as the format string, the safe call passes it as an argument of a constant format. The page lists the attack under Injection with Code Injection as a related attack and input validation as the related control.
claims.verified_by: Read in full from a file fetched with raw.githubusercontent.com at the pinned commit. The lesson does not run %n.

claims.claim_vi: Session fixation, per OWASP: the attacker obtains or invents a session ID, induces the victim to authenticate with it, then uses it; it works when the application does not assign a new session ID at authentication; the ID can reach the victim through a URL, a hidden form field or a cookie set by injected script or a Set-Cookie header.
claims.verified_by: Read in full from a file fetched with raw.githubusercontent.com at the pinned commit.

claims.claim_vi: OWASP Session Management: the session ID must be renewed after any privilege level change, mandatory against session fixation and independent of HTTP or HTTPS; strict session management accepts only IDs the application generated (permissive accepts any ID); the session ID binds the user's authentication to HTTP traffic with the data held server side; TLS does not protect against session ID prediction, brute force, client-side tampering or fixation, but does effectively protect against interception or theft of session IDs through a man-in-the-middle attack; session IDs need at least 64 bits of entropy against brute-force guessing.
claims.section: Introduction; Transport Layer Security; Permissive and Strict; Renew the Session ID
claims.verified_by: Read in full from a file fetched with raw.githubusercontent.com at the pinned commit.

claims.claim_vi: Observed with a toy in-memory session store (no network): if the server keeps the session ID after login, an attacker who knows that ID sees the victim's account when the ID was issued by the server (strict or permissive) and, for an ID the attacker made up, only in permissive mode; if the server issues a new ID at login and discards the old one, the attacker sees nothing in all four combinations of rotate and strict. The model does not simulate how the ID reaches the victim's browser.
claims.section: Renew the Session ID After Any Privilege Level Change
claims.verified_by: No external page reports this output; observed by executing the script on the authoring machine (Python 3.13.16). Script exp2_fixation.py, eight cases.

claims.claim_vi: MDN's TCP handshake entry: the three-way handshake is SYN, SYN-ACK, ACK, happens after a DNS lookup and before the TLS handshake when a secure connection is created.
claims.verified_by: Read in full from a file fetched with raw.githubusercontent.com at the pinned commit.

claims.claim_vi: The Linux documentation: tcp_max_syn_backlog is the maximal number of remembered connection requests (SYN_RECV) that have not received an acknowledgment from the connecting client; tcp_syncookies sends syncookies when the syn backlog queue of a socket overflows, to prevent the common SYN flood attack (default 1), is a fallback facility not meant to help servers under legitimate load, and seriously violates the TCP protocol and does not allow TCP extensions; tcp_synack_retries sets how many times SYNACKs are retransmitted for a passive connection attempt (default 5, final timeout after 63 seconds), so how long a half-open entry is kept is configurable.
claims.verified_by: Read in full from a file fetched with raw.githubusercontent.com at the pinned commit. That the time entries are kept can be tuned through tcp_synack_retries is the author's reading of that entry.

claims.claim_vi: That a SYN cookie is a value derived from a secret and the client's address, letting the server remember nothing until the client answers, is general knowledge; the Linux entry read does not describe the mechanism.
claims.verified_by: Author's general knowledge; not checked against a source that was reachable.

claims.claim_vi: MDN's Denial of Service entry lists SYN flooding attack among DoS types, and the Linux documentation calls it the 'SYN flood attack'.
claims.verified_by: Read in full from a file fetched with raw.githubusercontent.com at the pinned commit.

claims.claim_vi: Observed on 127.0.0.1 (random port chosen by the operating system): a one-worker server with listen backlog 2 and eight idle client sockets that only connect: when the worker waits for ever, 4 of the 8 sockets connected within 0.5 s, and a legitimate client could not connect within 3 s; when the worker drops a connection after 0.2 s of silence, 7 sockets connected and the legitimate client was answered after 0.5 s; with no idle sockets the answer was immediate. Three runs gave the same result. These connections complete the handshake, so this is not a SYN flood.
claims.verified_by: No external page reports this output; observed by executing the script on the authoring machine (Python 3.13.16). Script exp1_loopback.py; one machine, one measurement series.

claims.claim_vi: Observed with an in-memory model of a half-open queue (capacity 8, 40 ticks, one legitimate SYN per tick, random arrival order with a fixed seed): with 4 or 10 never-answering SYNs per tick, a queue-only policy with entries living 5 ticks let 15 and 7 of 40 legitimate clients connect; entries living 1 tick, 40 and 29; a policy that sends a stateless cookie when the queue is full, 40 and 40. The 40 follows from how the model is built (attackers never answer) and says nothing about real SYN cookies.
claims.verified_by: No external page reports this output; observed by executing the script on the authoring machine (Python 3.13.16). Script exp1b_synqueue_model.py; deterministic (identical output on repeated runs); no packets involved.

claims.claim_vi: OWASP describes a man-in-the-middle attack on an HTTP transaction as targeting the TCP connection, splitting it into two connections so the attacker acts as a proxy; its tools for local networks include ARP spoofing; the related controls are HTTPS with HSTS, secure session management and certificate validation. MDN describes the attacker setting up a wireless access point in a public place such as a cafe or airport, and gives HTTPS (HTTP over TLS) as the primary defence.
claims.section: Description; MITM attack tools; Related Controls

claims.claim_vi: OWASP's TLS cheat sheet lists what TLS provides: confidentiality (protection against attackers reading the traffic), integrity and server authentication. That TLS does not prevent someone from tapping the line, only from reading what is captured, is the author's reasoning from that list.
claims.verified_by: Read in full from a file fetched with raw.githubusercontent.com at the pinned commit.

claims.claim_vi: MDN's session hijacking entry covers stealing a valid session ID and TCP session hijacking, in which an attacker takes over a TCP session mid-session; it lists generating a new session ID after successful login among protections.
claims.verified_by: Read in full from a file fetched with raw.githubusercontent.com at the pinned commit.

claims.claim_vi: OWASP describes brute force as making requests to a server with predetermined values and analysing the response, often against authentication and to discover hidden content, sent as GET and POST requests; OWASP's session guidance also names brute-force guessing of session IDs.
claims.verified_by: Read in full from a file fetched with raw.githubusercontent.com at the pinned commit. The session-ID statement is in the Session Management cheat sheet read in the same way.

claims.claim_vi: OSI is a reference model used to teach and name layers, while the Internet runs the TCP/IP protocol suite, which merges layers 5 to 7 into one application layer.
claims.verified_by: Author's general knowledge; not checked against a source (RFC and encyclopedia sites were not reachable). OWASP regrouping the seven layers into three surfaces is read at the cited section.

design_notes_vi: Hai khung thẻ chia bảy tầng thành phía chương trình (7, 6, 5) và phía đường truyền (4, 3, 2, 1), mỗi thẻ một đòn và một cách đỡ; khung cuối là bốn ghi chú về chỗ cách xếp tầng chỉ là quy ước. Không dùng ảnh nguồn.
source_deviations: The source lists only attacks; the lesson adds one defence per layer from OWASP and Linux documentation and marks where the layer mapping is conventional or contestable.
The source's 'Pushing' appears in no source read; the lesson says it may be a typo for phishing (the author's guess), which MDN describes as social engineering not tied to a network layer.

The source's 'malware injection', 'malicious code injection' and 'encoding/decoding vulnerabilities' do not appear in the sources read; the lesson uses the format string attack, which OWASP lists under injection, for the presentation layer.
The source writes 'SYN/ACK flood' at the transport layer; MDN and the Linux documentation call the attack a SYN flood, and the lesson uses that name.

The source puts session hijacking, session fixation and brute force at the session layer; OWASP describes them as attacks on the web application's session or on passwords and hidden pages, so the lesson calls the placement conventional.

The source puts man-in-the-middle only at the transport layer; OWASP describes it as splitting the TCP connection, with ARP-spoofing tools in local networks and TLS above TCP as the defence, and the lesson presents it as spanning layers.

The source lists DDoS at the application and network layers only; OWASP's classification has three surfaces (application, session or protocol, network or volumetric), and the lesson says DDoS has no single layer.

Route table manipulation, VLAN hopping, MAC address spoofing, physical tampering and electromagnetic interference are listed by the source but not explained in the lesson, because no independent source about them was read.
